author: Augustine
source_text: illae quibus tenere cogebar Aeneae nescio cuius errores, oblitus errorum meorum, et plorare Didonem mortuam, quia se occidit ab amore.
question: Cuius reginae mortem, quae se ab amore occidit, Augustinus puer in schola legens flebat?
question_en: Over which queen's death, who killed herself out of love, did the boy Augustine weep as he read in school?
derivation: The celebrated detail of Conf. 1: the boy wept over Dido's death ('plorare Didonem mortuam, quia se occidit ab amore'). Anchored to Augustine + the named queen Dido; the question's description (a queen who killed herself for love) alone fixes the referent. Single-name answer supported verbatim. Closed-book (one of the most-quoted episodes in the Confessions).

author: Augustine
source_text: illae quibus tenere cogebar Aeneae nescio cuius errores, oblitus errorum meorum, et plorare Didonem mortuam, quia se occidit ab amore.
question: Cuius viri errores Augustinus puer in schola ediscere cogebatur?
question_en: Whose wanderings was the boy Augustine forced to learn by heart in school?
derivation: The wandering hero whose 'errores' Augustine was compelled to memorize is named in the text ('Aeneae nescio cuius errores'). Entity-anchored to Augustine's schooling + the named hero Aeneas; single-name answer supported verbatim. Closed-book autobiographical fact.

author: Augustine
source_text: quid autem erat causae cur graecas litteras oderam, quibus puerulus imbuebar? ne nunc quidem mihi satis exploratum est. adamaveram enim latinas, non quas primi magistri sed quas docent qui grammatici vocantur.
question: Cum latinas litteras adamavisset, quas litteras Augustinus puer se odisse confitetur?
question_en: Although he had come to love Latin letters, which letters does Augustine confess he hated as a boy?
derivation: The well-known biographical fact that Augustine loved Latin but hated Greek as a schoolboy ('cur graecas litteras oderam ... adamaveram enim latinas'). Anchored to Augustine + the two named languages; clean which-language answer supported verbatim. Indirect statement 'se odisse' under 'confitetur'; concessive cum-clause with pluperfect subjunctive 'adamavisset'. Closed-book (Augustine's poor Greek is a standard fact about him).

author: Augustine
source_text: proponebatur enim mihi negotium, animae meae satis inquietum praemio laudis et dedecoris vel plagarum metu, ut dicerem verba Iunonis irascentis et dolentis quod non posset Italia Teucrorum avertere regem, quae numquam Iunonem dixisse audieram.
question: Cuius deae verba, irascentis et dolentis quod Teucrorum regem ab Italia avertere non posset, Augustino puero in schola dicenda proponebantur?
question_en: Whose words — those of a goddess angry and grieving that she could not turn the king of the Trojans away from Italy — was the boy Augustine set in school to declaim?
derivation: Augustine's school declamation exercise: putting into prose the angry speech of a goddess who could not keep the Trojan king from Italy ('verba Iunonis irascentis et dolentis quod non posset Italia Teucrorum avertere regem'). The description alone determines Juno (the Aeneid's divine antagonist), making it closed-book via both the Confessions and basic mythology. Single-name answer supported verbatim; anchored to Augustine's schooling + the named goddess and the Teucri/Italia.

author: Augustine
source_text: pariter remeabamus in Africam. et cum apud Ostia Tiberina essemus, mater defuncta est.
question: In quo loco mater Augustini mortua est, cum in Africam redire pararent?
question_en: In what place did Augustine's mother die, as they were preparing to return to Africa?
derivation: Canonical fact of Book 9: Monica dies at Ostia as the party heads back to Africa. Anchored to Augustine + his mother + the return to Africa; single place answer supported verbatim by 'cum apud Ostia Tiberina essemus, mater defuncta est.' Closed-book, one of the most famous deaths in the Confessions.

author: Augustine
source_text: ut quotquot haec legerint, meminerint ad altare tuum Monnicae, famulae tuae, cum Patricio, quondam eius coniuge, per quorum carnem introduxisti me in hanc vitam, quemadmodum nescio.
question: Quo nomine appellatur mater Augustini, quae apud Ostia mortua est?
question_en: By what name is Augustine's mother, who died at Ostia, called?
derivation: Augustine names his mother only here at the close of Book 9. Anchored to Augustine + his mother; single-name answer supported by 'Monnicae, famulae tuae... per quorum carnem introduxisti me in hanc vitam.' Closed-book (Monica is among the most famous mothers in literature). Spelling 'Monnica' per the text (also Monica).

author: Augustine
source_text: ut quotquot haec legerint, meminerint ad altare tuum Monnicae, famulae tuae, cum Patricio, quondam eius coniuge, per quorum carnem introduxisti me in hanc vitam, quemadmodum nescio.
question: Quo nomine appellatur pater Augustini, maritus Monnicae?
question_en: By what name is Augustine's father, the husband of Monnica, called?
derivation: Patricius is named as Monnica's husband and Augustine's parent ('cum Patricio, quondam eius coniuge, per quorum carnem introduxisti me'). Anchored to Augustine + Monnica; single-name answer. Also named at 9.9.19. Closed-book biographical fact.

author: Augustine
source_text: adiunximus etiam nobis puerum Adeodatum ex me natum carnaliter de peccato meo. tu bene feceras eum.
question: Quo nomine appellatur filius quem Augustinus carnaliter genuit?
question_en: By what name is the son whom Augustine begot in the flesh called?
derivation: Augustine's natural son, joined to the group and baptized with him and Alypius at Milan. Anchored to Augustine; single-name answer supported verbatim by 'puerum Adeodatum ex me natum carnaliter.' Closed-book.

author: Augustine
source_text: adiunximus etiam nobis puerum Adeodatum ex me natum carnaliter de peccato meo. tu bene feceras eum. annorum erat ferme quindecim et ingenio praeveniebat multos graves et doctos viros.
question: Quot fere annos natus erat Adeodatus, Augustini filius, eo tempore quo baptizatus est?
question_en: About how many years old was Adeodatus, Augustine's son, at the time he was baptized?
derivation: Number fact anchored to Adeodatus (Augustine's son) at the time of the Milan baptism. Answer mirrors the source's approximative 'ferme' ('annorum erat ferme quindecim'). Short, verifiable, closed-book.

author: Augustine
source_text: est liber noster qui inscribitur 'de magistro': ipse ibi mecum loquitur. tu scis illius esse sensa omnia quae inseruntur ibi ex persona conlocutoris mei, cum esset in annis sedecim.
question: Quo titulo inscribitur liber Augustini in quo filius eius Adeodatus conlocutor inducitur?
question_en: Under what title is the book of Augustine in which his son Adeodatus is brought in as interlocutor inscribed?
derivation: Augustine states that in his dialogue De magistro the interlocutor's words are his son's ('ex persona conlocutoris mei'). Anchored to Augustine + Adeodatus; single title answer supported verbatim. Closed-book (De Magistro is a well-known work).

author: Augustine
source_text: relicto rure Mediolanium remeavimus. placuit et Alypio renasci in te mecum iam induto humilitate sacramentis tuis congrua et fortissimo domitori corporis, usque ad Italicum solum glaciale nudo pede obterendum insolito ausu.
question: Quis amicus Augustini una cum eo Mediolani baptizatus est?
question_en: Which friend of Augustine was baptized at Milan together with him?
derivation: Alypius decided to be 'reborn' (baptized) along with Augustine on their return to Milan ('relicto rure Mediolanium remeavimus. placuit et Alypio renasci in te mecum'). Anchored to Augustine + Milan; single-name answer. Closed-book (Alypius is Augustine's well-known companion).

author: Augustine
source_text: et insinuavi per litteras antistiti tuo, viro sancto Ambrosio, pristinos errores meos et praesens votum meum, ut moneret quid mihi potissimum de libris tuis legendum esset, quo percipiendae tantae gratiae paratior aptiorque fierem. at ille iussit Esaiam prophetam, credo, quod prae ceteris evangelii vocationisque gentium sit praenuntiator apertior.
question: Quem prophetam Augustino legendum antistes Ambrosius iussit?
question_en: Which prophet did the bishop Ambrose order Augustine to read?
derivation: Augustine asked the bishop Ambrose what to read; Ambrose directed him to Isaiah ('at ille iussit Esaiam prophetam'). Anchored to Ambrose (named 'antistiti tuo, viro sancto Ambrosio') + Augustine; single-name answer supported verbatim. Closed-book.

author: Augustine
source_text: ergo die nono aegritudinis suae, quinquagesimo et sexto anno aetatis suae, tricesimo et tertio aetatis meae, anima illa religiosa et pia corpore soluta est.
question: Quoto anno aetatis suae Monnica, mater Augustini, mortua est?
question_en: In which year of her age did Monnica, Augustine's mother, die?
derivation: Number fact anchored to Monnica: she died in the 56th year of her age ('quinquagesimo et sexto anno aetatis suae'). Short, verifiable, closed-book.

author: Augustine
source_text: ergo die nono aegritudinis suae, quinquagesimo et sexto anno aetatis suae, tricesimo et tertio aetatis meae, anima illa religiosa et pia corpore soluta est.
question: Quotum annum aetatis agebat Augustinus cum mater eius Monnica mortua est?
question_en: What year of his age was Augustine in when his mother Monnica died?
derivation: Number fact anchored to Augustine: he was in his 33rd year at his mother's death ('tricesimo et tertio aetatis meae'). Distinct referent from the mother's age; short, verifiable, closed-book.

author: Augustine
source_text: ergo die nono aegritudinis suae, quinquagesimo et sexto anno aetatis suae, tricesimo et tertio aetatis meae, anima illa religiosa et pia corpore soluta est.
question: Quoto die aegritudinis suae Monnica mortua est?
question_en: On which day of her illness did Monnica die?
derivation: Number fact anchored to Monnica: she died on the ninth day of her illness ('die nono aegritudinis suae'). Short, verifiable, closed-book. (Note 9.11.27's 'vix intra quinque dies... decubuit febribus' refers to the acute febrile phase; the explicit death-statement gives the ninth day of the whole illness.)

author: Augustine
source_text: tunc memorato antistiti tuo per visum aperuisti quo loco laterent martyrum corpora Protasii et Gervasii, quae per tot annos incorrupta in thesauro secreti tui reconderas, unde opportune promeres ad cohercendam rabiem femineam sed regiam.
question: Quorum martyrum corpora Ambrosius Mediolani, per visum sibi monstrata, invenit?
question_en: The bodies of which martyrs, revealed to him through a vision, did Ambrose find at Milan?
derivation: The 'antistes' is Ambrose (named in 9.7.15). Through a vision he found the bodies of the martyrs Protasius and Gervasius ('martyrum corpora Protasii et Gervasii'), later moved to the Ambrosian basilica. Anchored to Ambrose + Milan; two-name answer supported verbatim. Closed-book (the inventio of SS. Gervasius and Protasius).

author: Augustine
source_text: recordatus sum veridicos versus Ambrosii tui. tu es enim, deus, creator omnium, polique rector vestiens diem decoro lumine, noctem sopora gratia, artus solutos ut quies reddat laboris usui mentesque fessas allevet luctuque solvat anxios.
question: A quo auctore compositi sunt versus 'Deus creator omnium' quos Augustinus post matris suae mortem recordatus est?
question_en: By what author were the verses 'Deus creator omnium,' which Augustine recalled after his mother's death, composed?
derivation: Augustine recalls 'veridicos versus Ambrosii tui' beginning 'deus, creator omnium' — the Ambrosian hymn. Anchored to Augustine + Ambrose; single-name answer supported verbatim. Closed-book (a famous Ambrosian hymn). Source_text normalized: per-line quotation marks and a stray bracket stripped, hymn lines joined.

author: Augustine
source_text: fidelis promissor reddis Verecundo pro rure illo eius Cassiciaco, ubi ab aestu saeculi requievimus in te, amoenitatem sempiterne virentis paradisi tui.
question: Quo nomine appellabatur rus Verecundi ubi Augustinus cum suis post conversionem requievit?
question_en: By what name was the country estate of Verecundus, where Augustine and his companions rested after their conversion, called?
derivation: Verecundus's estate where Augustine's party retreated is named Cassiciacum ('pro rure illo eius Cassiciaco, ubi... requievimus'). Anchored to Verecundus + Augustine; single place-name answer (ablative 'Cassiciaco' in text, nom. Cassiciacum). Closed-book (the Cassiciacum retreat/dialogues are famous in Augustine's biography).

author: Caesar
source_text: Gallos ab Aquitanis Garumna flumen, a Belgis Matrona et Sequana dividit.
question: Quod flumen, ut Caesar scribit, Gallos ab Aquitanis dividit?
question_en: Which river, as Caesar writes, divides the Gauls from the Aquitani?
derivation: Geography fact of the famous opening chapter. Anchored to the Gauls, the Aquitani, and Caesar; single river answer supported verbatim by 'Gallos ab Aquitanis Garumna flumen ... dividit'. Closed-book staple of Latin geography.

author: Caesar
source_text: Apud Helvetios longe nobilissimus fuit et ditissimus Orgetorix.
question: Quis apud Helvetios longe nobilissimus ac ditissimus fuit?
question_en: Who was by far the noblest and richest man among the Helvetii?
derivation: Name fact anchored to the Helvetii; single named answer supported verbatim. Orgetorix is the well-known instigator of the Helvetian migration; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Pro multitudine autem hominum et pro gloria belli atque fortitudinis angustos se fines habere arbitrabantur, qui in longitudinem milia passuum CCXL, in latitudinem CLXXX patebant.
question: Quot milia passuum in longitudinem fines Helvetiorum patebant?
question_en: How many miles in length did the territory of the Helvetii extend?
derivation: Measure fact anchored to the Helvetii; number answer (CCXL = 240) supported verbatim, the width being CLXXX. The guidelines list exactly this kind of distance fact as a target.

author: Caesar
source_text: Id hoc facilius iis persuasit, quod undique loci natura Helvetii continentur: una ex parte flumine Rheno latissimo atque altissimo, qui agrum Helvetium a Germanis dividit; altera ex parte monte Iura altissimo, qui est inter Sequanos et Helvetios; tertia lacu Lemanno et flumine Rhodano, qui provinciam nostram ab Helvetiis dividit.
question: Qui mons inter Sequanos et Helvetios situs est?
question_en: Which mountain lies between the Sequani and the Helvetii?
derivation: Geography fact anchored to the Sequani and Helvetii; single answer supported verbatim by 'monte Iura altissimo, qui est inter Sequanos et Helvetios'. Closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Itemque Dumnorigi Haeduo, fratri Diviciaci, qui eo tempore principatum in civitate obtinebat ac maxime plebi acceptus erat, ut idem conaretur persuadet eique filiam suam in matrimonium dat.
question: Cui Orgetorix filiam suam in matrimonium dedit?
question_en: To whom did Orgetorix give his daughter in marriage?
derivation: Relation fact anchored to Orgetorix; single named answer supported verbatim by 'eique filiam suam in matrimonium dat' (the antecedent being Dumnorix). Dumnorix is a major figure of Book 1; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Caesar, quod memoria tenebat L. Cassium consulem occisum exercitumque eius ab Helvetiis pulsum et sub iugum missum, concedendum non putabat.
question: Quem consulem Romanum Helvetii antea occiderant eiusque exercitum sub iugum miserant?
question_en: Which Roman consul had the Helvetii earlier killed, and sent his army under the yoke?
derivation: Historical name fact anchored to the Helvetii and a consul; single named answer supported verbatim. The defeat of L. Cassius (107 BC) is closed-book history echoed again in 1.12.

author: Caesar
source_text: Interea ea legione quam secum habebat militibusque, qui ex provincia convenerant, a lacu Lemanno, qui in flumen Rhodanum influit, ad montem Iuram, qui fines Sequanorum ab Helvetiis dividit, milia passuum XVIIII murum in altitudinem pedum sedecim fossamque perducit.
question: Quot milia passuum longum murum Caesar a lacu Lemanno ad montem Iuram perduxit?
question_en: How many miles long was the wall Caesar built from Lake Geneva to the Jura?
derivation: Number/engineering fact anchored to Caesar, Lake Leman, and the Jura; answer (XVIIII = 19) supported verbatim (the height being sixteen feet). Closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Flumen est Arar, quod per fines Haeduorum et Sequanorum in Rhodanum influit, incredibili lenitate, ita ut oculis in utram partem fluat iudicari non possit.
question: In quod flumen Ararim influere Caesar scribit?
question_en: Into which river does Caesar write the Arar flows?
derivation: Geography fact anchored to the Arar (Saone); single answer supported verbatim by 'in Rhodanum influit'. Indirect statement (Ararim influere) governed by scribit; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Is pagus appellabatur Tigurinus; nam omnis civitas Helvetia in quattuor pagos divisa est. Hic pagus unus, cum domo exisset, patrum nostrorum memoria L. Cassium consulem interfecerat et eius exercitum sub iugum miserat.
question: Quo nomine appellabatur pagus Helvetius qui L. Cassium consulem interfecerat?
question_en: What was the name of the Helvetian canton that had killed the consul Lucius Cassius?
derivation: Name fact anchored to the Helvetii and to Cassius; single named answer supported verbatim ('Is pagus appellabatur Tigurinus' + 'L. Cassium consulem interfecerat'). Closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Legatos ad eum mittunt; cuius legationis Divico princeps fuit, qui bello Cassiano dux Helvetiorum fuerat.
question: Quis dux Helvetiorum bello Cassiano fuerat et postea legationi ad Caesarem missae praefuit?
question_en: Who had been the leader of the Helvetii in the Cassian war and later headed the embassy to Caesar?
derivation: Name fact doubly anchored (Helvetii, the Cassian war, Caesar); single named answer supported verbatim by 'Divico princeps fuit, qui bello Cassiano dux Helvetiorum fuerat'. Closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Qui summo magistratui praeerat, quem vergobretum appellant Haedui, qui creatur annuus et vitae necisque in suos habet potestatem.
question: Quo nomine Haedui summum magistratum suum appellant?
question_en: By what name do the Haedui call their supreme magistrate?
derivation: Institution/custom fact anchored to the Haedui; single named answer supported verbatim by 'quem vergobretum appellant Haedui'. A distinctive named office (annual, with power of life and death); closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: A Bibracte, oppido Haeduorum longe maximo et copiosissimo, non amplius milibus passuum XVIII aberat.
question: Quod oppidum Haeduorum longe maximum et copiosissimum fuisse Caesar scribit?
question_en: Which town does Caesar write was by far the largest and richest of the Haedui?
derivation: Place fact anchored to the Haedui; single named answer supported verbatim by 'Bibracte, oppido Haeduorum longe maximo et copiosissimo'. Indirect statement (fuisse) under scribit; the iconic Aeduan oppidum, closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: In castris Helvetiorum tabulae repertae sunt litteris Graecis confectae et ad Caesarem relatae, quibus in tabulis nominatim ratio confecta erat, qui numerus domo exisset eorum qui arma ferre possent, et item separatim, quot pueri, senes mulieresque.
question: Quibus litteris tabulae in castris Helvetiorum repertae confectae erant?
question_en: In what script were the tablets found in the camp of the Helvetii written?
derivation: A striking, much-cited fact anchored to the Helvetian camp; single answer supported verbatim by 'tabulae ... litteris Graecis confectae'. Closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Ariovistus, rex Germanorum, in eorum finibus consedisset tertiamque partem agri Sequani, qui esset optimus totius Galliae, occupavisset.
question: Quis erat rex Germanorum qui in finibus Sequanorum consedit?
question_en: Who was the king of the Germani who settled in the territory of the Sequani?
derivation: Name fact anchored to the Germani and the Sequani; single named answer supported verbatim by 'Ariovistus, rex Germanorum, in eorum finibus consedisset'. Ariovistus is the central antagonist of Book 1; closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Nuntiatum est ei Ariovistum cum suis omnibus copiis ad occupandum Vesontionem, quod est oppidum maximum Sequanorum, contendere.
question: Quod oppidum, Sequanorum maximum, Ariovistus occupare contendit?
question_en: Which town, the largest of the Sequani, did Ariovistus hasten to seize?
derivation: Place fact anchored to the Sequani and Ariovistus; single named answer supported verbatim by 'Vesontionem, quod est oppidum maximum Sequanorum'. Closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Apud Germanos ea consuetudo esset ut matres familiae eorum sortibus et vaticinationibus declararent utrum proelium committi ex usu esset necne; eas ita dicere: non esse fas Germanos superare, si ante novam lunam proelio contendissent.
question: Ante quid Germanos vincere fas non esse matres familiae declarabant?
question_en: Before what did the German matrons declare it was not right (fas) for the Germani to win?
derivation: Ethnographic custom fact anchored to the Germani; short answer supported verbatim by 'non esse fas Germanos superare, si ante novam lunam proelio contendissent'. Distinctive and closed-book.

author: Caesar
source_text: Sed de his duobus generibus alterum est druidum, alterum equitum.
question: Quae duo genera hominum honoratorum apud Gallos esse Caesar tradit?
question_en: Which two classes of honored men does Caesar report exist among the Gauls?
derivation: The famous fact that among Gauls of rank there are two privileged orders. Anchored to Caesar + the Gauls; single, verifiable two-name answer supported verbatim (alterum druidum, alterum equitum). Indirect statement (genera... esse) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Disciplina in Britannia reperta atque inde in Galliam translata esse existimatur, et nunc, qui diligentius eam rem cognoscere volunt, plerumque illo discendi causa proficiscuntur.
question: Ubi disciplinam druidum repertam esse Caesar tradit?
question_en: Where does Caesar report that the discipline of the druids was discovered?
derivation: Caesar's claim about the origin of druidic disciplina. Anchored to the druids; single place-name answer supported verbatim (in Britannia reperta). Indirect statement (disciplinam... repertam esse) under tradit; closed-book, oft-cited.

author: Caesar
source_text: Tantis excitati praemiis et sua sponte multi in disciplinam conveniunt et a parentibus propinquisque mittuntur. Magnum ibi numerum versuum ediscere dicuntur. Itaque annos nonnulli vicenos in disciplina permanent.
question: Quot annos nonnulli in druidum disciplina permaneant Caesar tradit?
question_en: How many years does Caesar report that some remain in the druids' training?
derivation: Length-of-training number fact. Anchored to the druidic disciplina; single number answer supported verbatim (annos... vicenos). Indirect question (permaneant, subj.) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Neque fas esse existimant ea litteris mandare, cum in reliquis fere rebus, publicis privatisque rationibus Graecis litteris utantur.
question: Quibus litteris Galli in publicis privatisque rationibus utantur Caesar scribit?
question_en: Which script does Caesar say the Gauls used for their public and private accounts?
derivation: Notable fact that, while not committing druidic lore to writing, the Gauls used Greek script for records. Anchored to the Gauls + accounts; verifiable answer supported verbatim (Graecis litteris utantur). Indirect question (utantur, subj.) under scribit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Deum maxime Mercurium colunt. Huius sunt plurima simulacra: hunc omnium inventorem artium ferunt, hunc viarum atque itinerum ducem, hunc ad quaestus pecuniae mercaturasque habere vim maximam arbitrantur.
question: Quem deum Gallos maxime colere Caesar tradit?
question_en: Which god does Caesar report the Gauls worship most?
derivation: The most-cited fact of the Gallic pantheon section. Anchored to Caesar + the Gauls; single name answer supported verbatim (Deum maxime Mercurium colunt). Indirect statement (Gallos colere) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Galli se omnes ab Dite patre prognatos praedicant idque ab druidibus proditum dicunt.
question: A quo deo Galli se omnes prognatos esse praedicant, ut Caesar scribit?
question_en: From which god do the Gauls proclaim they are all descended, as Caesar writes?
derivation: Iconic claim of Gallic descent. Anchored to the Gauls; single divine-name answer supported verbatim (ab Dite patre prognatos). Direct question with the source's acc.+inf. (se prognatos esse) plus parenthetical attribution.

author: Caesar
source_text: Ob eam causam spatia omnis temporis non numero dierum sed noctium finiunt; dies natales et mensum et annorum initia sic observant ut noctem dies subsequatur.
question: Utrum numero dierum an noctium Galli omnia temporis spatia finire soleant Caesar tradit?
question_en: Does Caesar report that the Gauls reckon all spans of time by the count of days or of nights?
derivation: The well-known Celtic night-reckoning custom. Anchored to the Gauls; disjunctive question with a single verifiable answer supported verbatim (non numero dierum sed noctium). Indirect question (soleant, subj.) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Germani multum ab hac consuetudine differunt. Nam neque druides habent, qui rebus divinis praesint, neque sacrificiis student. Deorum numero eos solos ducunt, quos cernunt et quorum aperte opibus iuvantur, Solem et Vulcanum et Lunam, reliquos ne fama quidem acceperunt.
question: Quos solos deorum numero Germanos ducere Caesar tradit?
question_en: Which gods alone does Caesar report the Germani count among the gods?
answer_en: The Sun, Vulcan, and the Moon.
derivation: Specific German religious custom (contrast with the Gauls). Anchored to the Germani; complete three-name enumeration supported verbatim (Solem et Vulcanum et Lunam). Indirect statement (Germanos ducere) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Agriculturae non student, maiorque pars eorum victus in lacte, caseo, carne consistit.
question: In quibus rebus maiorem partem victus Germanorum consistere Caesar scribit?
question_en: In what does Caesar say the greater part of the Germani's food consists?
derivation: Specific German dietary custom. Anchored to the Germani; complete three-item enumeration supported verbatim (in lacte, caseo, carne consistit). Indirect statement (maiorem partem... consistere) under scribit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Itaque ea quae fertilissima Germaniae sunt loca circum Hercyniam silvam, quam Eratostheni et quibusdam Graecis fama notam esse video, quam illi Orcyniam appellant, Volcae Tectosages occupaverunt atque ibi consederunt.
question: Quam gentem Gallorum loca circum Hercyniam silvam occupavisse Caesar tradit?
question_en: Which Gallic people, according to Caesar, occupied the lands around the Hercynian forest?
derivation: Named-people fact about settlement around the Hercynian forest. Anchored to the Hercynian forest; single people-name answer supported verbatim (Volcae Tectosages occupaverunt). Indirect statement (gentem... occupavisse) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Huius Hercyniae silvae, quae supra demonstrata est, latitudo novem dierum iter expedito patet.
question: Quot dierum iter in latitudinem Hercyniam silvam patere Caesar tradit?
question_en: How many days' journey wide does Caesar report the Hercynian forest to be?
derivation: Measure fact for the Hercynian forest's breadth. Anchored to the Hercynian forest; single number answer supported verbatim (latitudo novem dierum iter ... patet). Indirect statement (silvam patere) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Sunt item, quae appellantur alces. Harum est consimilis capris figura et varietas pellium, sed magnitudine paulo antecedunt mutilaeque sunt cornibus et crura sine nodis articulisque habent neque quietis causa procumbunt.
question: Quas feras Hercyniae silvae crura sine nodis articulisque habere Caesar tradit?
question_en: Which beasts of the Hercynian forest does Caesar report have legs without knots or joints?
derivation: Named animal of the Hercynian forest with its signature feature (jointless legs). Anchored to the forest; single animal-name answer supported verbatim (alces ... crura sine nodis articulisque habent). Indirect statement (feras habere) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Tertium est genus eorum, qui uri appellantur. Hi sunt magnitudine paulo infra elephantos, specie et colore et figura tauri.
question: Quo animali uros magnitudine paulo inferiores esse Caesar scribit?
question_en: To which animal does Caesar report the uri (aurochs) are slightly inferior in size?
answer_en: Elephants (the uri are a little smaller than elephants).
derivation: Named animal of the Hercynian forest with a comparative-size fact. Anchored to the uri; single answer supported verbatim (magnitudine paulo infra elephantos). Indirect statement (uros inferiores esse) under scribit; abl. of comparison.

author: Caesar
source_text: per Arduennam silvam, quae est totius Galliae maxima atque ab ripis Rheni finibusque Treverorum ad Nervios pertinet milibusque amplius quingentis in longitudinem patet
question: Quam silvam totius Galliae maximam esse Caesar tradit?
question_en: Which forest does Caesar report is the largest in all Gaul?
derivation: Superlative geography fact. Anchored to Gaul; single place-name answer supported verbatim (quae est totius Galliae maxima). Indirect statement (silvam... esse) under tradit.

author: Caesar
source_text: Catuvolcus, rex dimidiae partis Eburonum, qui una cum Ambiorige consilium inierat, aetate iam confectus, cum laborem aut belli aut fugae ferre non posset, omnibus precibus detestatus Ambiorigem, qui eius consilii auctor fuisset, taxo, cuius magna in Gallia Germaniaque copia est, se exanimavit.
question: Qua re Catuvolcus, dimidiae partis Eburonum rex, se exanimaverit Caesar tradit?
question_en: With what did Catuvolcus, king of half the Eburones, kill himself, according to Caesar?
derivation: Named-person fact: the manner of Catuvolcus' suicide. Anchored to Catuvolcus + the Eburones; single answer supported verbatim (taxo ... se exanimavit). Indirect question (exanimaverit, subj.) under tradit.

author: Cato
source_text: Et virum bonum quom laudabant, ita laudabant: bonum agricolam bonumque colonum; amplissime laudari existimabatur qui ita laudabatur.
question: Quibus verbis maiores, ut Cato scribit, virum bonum amplissime laudabant?
question_en: With what words, as Cato writes, did the ancestors most highly praise a good man?
answer_en: A good farmer and a good husbandman.
derivation: The famous claim of the praefatio: the highest praise for a man was to call him 'bonum agricolam bonumque colonum.' Anchored to Cato + the maiores; the answer is the exact predicate phrase, supported verbatim. Closed-book: one of the most-quoted lines of Cato. Imperfect 'laudabant' kept indicative; 'ut Cato scribit' is a parenthetical author-frame.

author: Cato
source_text: At ex agricolis et viri fortissimi et milites strenuissimi gignuntur, maximeque pius quaestus stabilissimusque consequitur minimeque invidiosus, minimeque male cogitantes sunt qui in eo studio occupati sunt.
question: Ex quibus hominibus et viros fortissimos et milites strenuissimos gigni Cato adfirmat?
question_en: From which men does Cato assert that both the bravest men and the most vigorous soldiers are born?
derivation: Cato's celebrated claim that farmers are the source of the bravest men and most vigorous soldiers. Anchored to Cato + agricolae; single answer 'ex agricolis,' supported verbatim. Closed-book and widely quoted. Indirect statement: passive infinitive 'gigni' with accusative subjects under 'adfirmat.'

author: Cato
source_text: Maiores nostri sic habuerunt et ita in legibus posiverunt: furem dupli condemnari, foeneratorem quadrupli.
question: Quanti, ut Cato refert, maiores in legibus foeneratorem condemnari iusserunt?
question_en: For how much, as Cato reports, did the ancestors order in their laws that a usurer be condemned?
derivation: Preface's comparison: the laws condemned a thief to double, a usurer to quadruple — Cato's point that usury was judged worse than theft. Anchored to Cato + the maiores' laws; genitive-of-penalty answer 'quadrupli' supported verbatim ('foeneratorem quadrupli'). Closed-book datum on Roman attitudes to usury. 'condemnari' passive inf. with acc. subject under 'iusserunt.'

author: Cato
source_text: Praedium quod primum siet, si me rogabis, sic dicam: de omnibus agris optimoque loco iugera agri centum, vinea est prima, vel si vino multo est; secundo loco hortus irriguus; tertio salictum; quarto oletum; quinto pratum; sexto campus frumentarius; septimo silva caedua; octavo arbustum; nono glandaria silva.
question: Quod agri genus Cato inter omnia primo loco numerat?
question_en: Which kind of farmland does Cato rank first among all?
derivation: Cato's well-known ranking of the nine kinds of farmland, with the vineyard (vinea) first. Anchored to Cato; single answer 'vineam,' supported verbatim by 'vinea est prima.' Closed-book: a standard datum in discussions of Roman agronomy. Only the first place is asked (the full list would fail short-answer).

author: Cato
source_text: Quid est agrum bene colere? Bene arare. Quid secundum? Arare. Quid tertium? Stercorare.
question: Quid Cato primum esse dicit in agro bene colendo?
question_en: What does Cato say is the first thing in cultivating a field well?
derivation: Cato's celebrated catechism on good husbandry: first to plow well, second to plow, third to manure ('arare, arare, stercorare'). Anchored to Cato; single answer 'bene arare,' supported verbatim. Closed-book: among the most-quoted lines of Cato. Indirect statement under 'dicit.'

author: Cato
source_text: Brassica est quae omnibus holeribus antistat.
question: Quod holus Cato omnibus holeribus antistare scribit?
question_en: Which vegetable does Cato write surpasses all other vegetables?
derivation: Cato's famous superlative praise of the cabbage as the best of all vegetables, opening his cabbage-chapter. Anchored to Cato; single answer 'brassicam,' supported verbatim. Closed-book: Cato's enthusiasm for cabbage is well-known trivia (discussed e.g. by Pliny). 'antistare' + dative; acc. subject 'brassicam' under 'scribit.'

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Iuri operam daturum prius nosse oportet, unde nomen iuris descendat. est autem a iustitia appellatum: nam, ut eleganter celsus definit, ius est ars boni et aequi.
question: Quibus verbis Celsus, ut Ulpianus refert, ius definit?
answer: Ius est ars boni et aequi.
question_en: In what words does Celsus, as Ulpian reports, define law (ius)?
answer_en: Law is the art of the good and the equitable.
derivation: The single most-quoted definition of ius in Roman law, attributed by Ulpian to Celsus. Closed-book famous maxim, entity-anchored to Celsus, short verifiable answer present verbatim ('ius est ars boni et aequi').

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Ius naturale est, quod natura omnia animalia docuit: nam ius istud non humani generis proprium, sed omnium animalium, quae in terra, quae in mari nascuntur, avium quoque commune est.
question: Quomodo Ulpianus ius naturale definit?
question_en: How does Ulpian define natural law (ius naturale)?
answer_en: That which nature has taught all animals.
derivation: Ulpian's famous definition of ius naturale as the law nature taught all animals, not only mankind. Closed-book maxim, anchored to Ulpian + ius naturale, short answer verbatim from the source.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: et cum uno naturali nomine homines appellaremur, iure gentium tria genera esse coeperunt: liberi et his contrarium servi et tertium genus liberti, id est hi qui desierant esse servi.
question: Quae tria genera hominum iure gentium orta esse Ulpianus scribit?
question_en: Which three classes of men does Ulpian say arose by the law of nations (ius gentium)?
derivation: Ulpian: under ius gentium three classes of men arose — liberi, servi, liberti. Closed-book, anchored to Ulpian + ius gentium, three named-entity answer verbatim. Indirect statement (orta esse) governed by scribit.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Ius praetorium est, quod praetores introduxerunt adiuvandi vel supplendi vel corrigendi iuris civilis gratia propter utilitatem publicam. quod et honorarium dicitur ad honorem praetorum sic nominatum.
question: Cuius rei gratia praetores ius praetorium introduxisse Papinianus scribit?
answer: Adiuvandi vel supplendi vel corrigendi iuris civilis gratia.
question_en: For what purpose does Papinian say the praetors introduced praetorian law?
answer_en: For the sake of aiding, supplementing, or correcting the civil law.
derivation: Papinian's classic triad of the purposes of ius praetorium (adiuvandi, supplendi, corrigendi iuris civilis). Closed-book, anchored to Papinian + ius praetorium, answer verbatim. Indirect statement (introduxisse) governed by scribit.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Iustitia est constans et perpetua voluntas ius suum cuique tribuendi.
question: Quomodo Ulpianus iustitiam definit?
answer: Constans et perpetua voluntas ius suum cuique tribuendi.
question_en: How does Ulpian define justice (iustitia)?
answer_en: The constant and perpetual will to render to each his own right.
derivation: The canonical definition of iustitia (later opening Justinian's Institutes), quoted here from Ulpian. Closed-book maxim, anchored to Ulpian + iustitia, short answer verbatim.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Iuris praecepta sunt haec: honeste vivere, alterum non laedere, suum cuique tribuere.
question: Quae sunt tria iuris praecepta secundum Ulpianum?
answer: Honeste vivere, alterum non laedere, suum cuique tribuere.
question_en: What are the three precepts of law according to Ulpian?
answer_en: To live honourably, to harm no one, to render to each his own.
derivation: Ulpian's three iuris praecepta, among the most famous formulas in Western law. Closed-book, anchored to Ulpian + iuris praecepta, three-part answer verbatim.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Postea aucta ad aliquem modum civitate ipsum romulum traditur populum in triginta partes divisisse, quas partes curias appellavit propterea quod tunc reipublicae curam per sententias partium earum expediebat.
question: In quot partes Romulus populum divisisse traditur, quas curias appellavit, ut Pomponius scribit?
question_en: Into how many parts is Romulus said to have divided the people, which he called curiae, as Pomponius writes?
derivation: From Pomponius's history of law: Romulus divided the people into 30 curiae. Closed-book, anchored to Romulus + curiae, single number answer (triginta) verbatim; traditur keeps the 'it is reported' frame (nom.+inf. construction).

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Placuit publica auctoritate decem constitui viros, per quos peterentur leges a graecis civitatibus et civitas fundaretur legibus: quas in tabulas eboreas perscriptas pro rostris composuerunt, ut possint leges apertius percipi. qui ipsi animadverterunt aliquid deesse istis primis legibus ideoque sequenti anno alias duas ad easdem tabulas adiecerunt: et ita ex accedenti appellatae sunt leges duodecim tabularum.
question: Quot viri publica auctoritate constituti sunt, ut leges duodecim tabularum conderentur, secundum Pomponium?
question_en: How many men were appointed by public authority to establish the law of the Twelve Tables, according to Pomponius?
derivation: Pomponius: ten men (decemviri) were appointed and composed the Twelve Tables (two more tables added the following year giving the name). Closed-book, anchored to the Twelve Tables + decemviri, number answer (decem) verbatim from 'decem constitui viros'.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: itaque dictatores proditi sunt, a quibus nec provocandi ius fuit et quibus etiam capitis animadversio data est. hunc magistratum, quoniam summam potestatem habebat, non erat fas ultra sextum mensem retineri.
question: Ultra quot menses dictaturam retineri fas non erat secundum Pomponium?
question_en: Beyond how many months was it not lawful to retain the dictatorship, according to Pomponius?
derivation: Pomponius: the dictatorship, holding supreme power, could not lawfully be held beyond six months. Closed-book institutional fact, anchored to the dictatorship, number answer verbatim ('ultra sextum mensem').

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Post hos fuerunt publius mucius et brutus et manilius, qui fundaverunt ius civile. ex his publius mucius etiam decem libellos reliquit, brutus septem, manilius tres.
question: Qui tres iuris periti ius civile fundavisse a Pomponio dicuntur?
question_en: Which three jurists are said by Pomponius to have founded the civil law?
derivation: Pomponius names the three 'founders of ius civile' (qui fundaverunt ius civile): Publius Mucius Scaevola, Brutus, Manilius. Closed-book in legal history, three named-entity answer verbatim; dicuntur + nom.+inf. (fundavisse).

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Post hos fuit tiberius coruncanius, ut dixi, qui primus profiteri coepit: cuius tamen scriptum nullum exstat, sed responsa complura et memorabilia eius fuerunt.
question: Quis primus ius publice profiteri coepisse a Pomponio traditur?
question_en: Who, according to Pomponius, was the first to begin teaching law publicly?
derivation: Pomponius: Tiberius Coruncanius was the first to teach/give responsa publicly (profiteri). Closed-book historical fact, single named-entity answer, supported by 'qui primus profiteri coepit' (cf. 1.2.2.35 'ante Tiberium Coruncanium publice professum neminem').

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Legis virtus haec est imperare vetare permittere punire.
question: Quae sunt quattuor legis virtutes secundum Modestinum?
question_en: What are the four powers (functions) of law according to Modestinus?
answer_en: To command, to forbid, to permit, to punish.
derivation: Modestinus's four functions of law (imperare, vetare, permittere, punire). Closed-book maxim, anchored to Modestinus + lex, four-part answer verbatim.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
locus: Justinian, Digesta 1.3.31 (Ulpianus 13 ad l. iul. et pap.)
source_text: Princeps legibus solutus est: augusta autem licet legibus soluta non est, principes tamen eadem illi privilegia tribuunt, quae ipsi habent.
question: Quid de principe quoad leges Ulpianus affirmat?
question_en: What does Ulpian assert about the emperor with respect to the laws?
answer_en: That the emperor is freed from (not bound by) the laws.
derivation: The maxim 'princeps legibus solutus est', foundational to later theories of sovereignty, stated here by Ulpian. Closed-book, anchored to Ulpian + princeps, short answer; indirect statement (Principem... solutum esse) governed by affirmat, supported verbatim.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Quod principi placuit, legis habet vigorem: utpote cum lege regia, quae de imperio eius lata est, populus ei et in eum omne suum imperium et potestatem conferat.
question: Quam vim habere id quod principi placuit Ulpianus tradit?
question_en: What force does Ulpian record that whatever pleases the emperor has?
derivation: Ulpian's maxim 'quod principi placuit, legis habet vigorem'. Closed-book, anchored to Ulpian + princeps, short answer 'legis vigorem' verbatim; indirect statement (id... habere) governed by tradit.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: Omne ius quo utimur vel ad personas pertinet vel ad res vel ad actiones.
question: Ad quae tria omne ius quo utimur pertinere Gaius scribit?
answer: Ad personas, ad res, ad actiones.
question_en: To which three things does Gaius say that all the law we use pertains?
answer_en: To persons, to things, and to actions.
derivation: Gaius's tripartite division of all law into personae, res, actiones — the organizing scheme of his Institutes. Closed-book, anchored to Gaius, three-part answer verbatim; indirect statement (pertinere) governed by scribit.

author: Justinian (Corpus Iuris Civilis)
source_text: In orbe romano qui sunt ex constitutione imperatoris antonini cives romani effecti sunt.
question: Cuius imperatoris constitutione omnes qui in orbe Romano erant cives Romani facti sunt, ut Ulpianus scribit?
question_en: By the constitution of which emperor did all who were in the Roman world become Roman citizens, as Ulpian writes?
derivation: Ulpian's record of the Constitutio Antoniniana (AD 212), by which Caracalla (Antoninus) granted citizenship to all free inhabitants of the empire. Closed-book famous historical fact, anchored to the emperor Antoninus, single named-entity answer verbatim ('ex constitutione imperatoris Antonini').

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Terrarum orbis universus in tres dividitur partes, Europam, Asiam, Africam.
question: In quot partes terrarum orbem universum dividi Plinius tradit, et quas?
answer: In tres partes: Europam, Asiam et Africam.
question_en: Into how many parts does Pliny say the whole world is divided, and which?
answer_en: Into three parts: Europe, Asia, and Africa.
derivation: Number-plus-names fact opening the geographical books. Anchored to the orbis terrarum; single verifiable answer (three named continents) supported verbatim. Indirect statement orbem dividi governed by tradit; closed-book because the tripartite division of the world is a commonplace of ancient geography.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: proximis autem faucibus utrimque inpositi montes coercent claustra, Abila Africae, Europae Calpe, laborum Herculis metae, quam ob causam indigenae columnas eius dei vocant.
question: Qui duo montes ad fauces oceani positi 'laborum Herculis metae' sive columnae Herculis a Plinio appellantur?
question_en: Which two mountains set on the strait of the ocean does Pliny call the 'limits of Hercules' labors,' i.e. the Pillars of Hercules?
derivation: Iconic Pillars of Hercules identification (Abila in Africa, Calpe in Europe). Two named entities, single checkable answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: among the best-known landmarks of ancient geography.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Hiberus amnis, navigabili commercio dives, ortus in Cantabris haut procul oppido Iuliobrica, per CCCCL p. fluens, navium per CCLX a Vareia oppido capax, quem propter universam Hispaniam Graeci appellavere Hiberiam.
question: A quo flumine Graeci universam Hispaniam Hiberiam appellaverunt secundum Plinium?
question_en: After which river did the Greeks name all of Spain 'Iberia,' according to Pliny?
derivation: Etymology of Iberia from the river Hiberus (Ebro). Entity-anchored (Spain, the Greeks, the river); single named answer supported verbatim by quem propter ... Graeci appellavere Hiberiam. Closed-book, recognizable geographic fact.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Pyrenaei montes Hispanias Galliasque disterminant promunturiis in duo diversa maria proiectis.
question: Qui montes Hispanias Galliasque inter se disterminant secundum Plinium?
question_en: Which mountains separate the Spains from the Gauls, according to Pliny?
derivation: Boundary fact: the Pyrenees divide Spain from Gaul. Two named regions, one mountain-range answer supported verbatim. Closed-book, textbook geography.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: praefari necessarium est auctorem nos Divum Augustum secuturos discriptionemque ab eo factam Italiae totius in regiones XI.
question: In quot regiones Divus Augustus Italiam totam discripsisse a Plinio traditur?
question_en: Into how many regions is the Deified Augustus said by Pliny to have divided all of Italy?
derivation: The famous Augustan division of Italy into eleven regiones, which structures the rest of the book. Anchored to Augustus + Italy; single number answer (XI) supported verbatim. Nominativus cum infinitivo (Augustus discripsisse traditur). Closed-book, attributed.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Est ergo folio maxime querno adsimulata, multo proceritate amplior quam latitudine.
question: Cui folio figuram Italiae maxime adsimilari Plinius scribit?
question_en: To which leaf does Pliny say the shape of Italy is most likened?
derivation: Pliny's well-known simile for the shape of Italy (an oak leaf). Subject (Italia) is the running topic; the question supplies it, making it decontextualizable. Short answer supported verbatim by folio querno adsimulata. Indirect statement governed by scribit.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: conplexa montes septem. ipsa dividitur in regiones XIIII, compita Larum CCLXV.
question: In quot regiones ipsa urbs Roma divisa est secundum Plinium?
question_en: Into how many regions is the city of Rome itself divided, according to Pliny?
derivation: The Augustan fourteen regiones of the city of Rome (distinct from the eleven regiones of Italy). Anchored to Rome; single number answer (XIV) supported verbatim. Question names urbs Roma so the source's ipsa is unambiguous. Closed-book.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Tiberis, ante Thyberis appellatus et prius Albula, e media fere longitudine Appennini finibus Arretinorum profluit.
question: Quo nomine Tiberis amnis antiquissime appellatus esse a Plinio dicitur?
question_en: By what name does Pliny say the river Tiber was called in earliest times?
derivation: The Tiber's oldest name. The text gives prius Albula (earlier than both Tiberis and Thyberis), so Albula is the earliest. Entity-anchored to the Tiber, single-name answer supported verbatim. Closed-book: a recurring antiquarian fact in Latin literature.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: fluvius Rubico, quondam finis Italiae.
question: Qui fluvius quondam finis Italiae fuisse a Plinio dicitur?
question_en: Which river does Pliny say was once the boundary of Italy?
derivation: The Rubicon as the former boundary of Italy (proper). Single named-river answer supported verbatim by Rubico, quondam finis Italiae. Closed-book and iconic (Caesar's crossing).

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Hirpinorum colonia una Beneventum auspicatius mutato nomine, quae quondam appellata Maleventum.
question: Quo nomine colonia Beneventum, ante nominis mutationem, quondam appellata est secundum Plinium?
question_en: By what name was the colony of Beneventum formerly called, before its name was changed, according to Pliny?
derivation: The renaming of Maleventum to the more auspicious Beneventum. Anchored to the town; single-name answer supported verbatim. Closed-book, frequently cited etymological/onomastic fact.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: oppidum Paestum, Graecis Posidonia appellatum, sinus Paestanus.
question: Quo nomine oppidum Paestum a Graecis appellatum esse Plinius tradit?
question_en: By what name do the Greeks call the town of Paestum, according to Pliny?
derivation: The Greek name of Paestum. Entity-anchored to the town; single-name answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and recognizable (the Greek colony Poseidonia).

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Padus, e gremio Vesuli montis celsissimum in cacumen Alpium elati finibus Ligurum Bagiennorum visendo fonte profluens condensque se cuniculo et in Forovibiensium agro iterum exoriens, nullo amnium claritate inferior, Graecis dictus Eridanus ac poena Phaethontis inlustratus.
question: Quo nomine Padus amnis a Graecis dictus esse a Plinio traditur?
question_en: By what name was the river Padus (Po) called by the Greeks, according to Pliny?
derivation: The Greek name of the Po, tied to the myth of Phaethon. Anchored to the Padus; single-name answer supported verbatim by Graecis dictus Eridanus. Closed-book, well-known.

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: Verum ante omnes claritate Sicilia, Sicania Thucydidi dicta, Trinacria pluribus aut Trinacia a triangula specie.
question: Quo nomine Sicilia a plerisque ob triangulam speciem appellata est secundum Plinium?
question_en: By what name is Sicily called by most people on account of its triangular shape, according to Pliny?
derivation: The name Trinacria for triangular Sicily. Anchored to Sicily; single-name answer supported verbatim by Trinacria ... a triangula specie. Closed-book, iconic (the island's three-cornered shape).

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: in hoc tractu interierunt Boi, quorum tribus CXII fuisse auctor est Cato, item Senones, qui ceperunt Romam.
question: Quae Gallorum gens Romam cepisse a Plinio memoratur?
question_en: Which Gallic people does Pliny record as having captured Rome?
derivation: Attributes the sack of Rome to the Senones. Anchored to Rome + the Gauls; single named-people answer supported verbatim by Senones, qui ceperunt Romam. Closed-book (Brennus' Gauls, 390 BC).

author: Pliny the Elder
source_text: ex quibus Laevi et Marici condidere Ticinum non procul a Pado, sicut Boi Transalpibus profecti Laudem Pompeiam, Insubres Mediolanum.
question: Quae gens Mediolanum condidisse secundum Plinium traditur?
question_en: Which people is said by Pliny to have founded Mediolanum (Milan)?
derivation: Founder fact: the Insubres founded Mediolanum (the verb condidere governs the list, sicut ... Insubres Mediolanum). Anchored to the city; single named-people answer supported verbatim. Closed-book and recognizable (Milan).

author: Suetonius
source_text: Natus est Augustus M. Tullio Cicerone C. Antonio conss. XIIII. Kal. Octob., paulo ante solis exortum, regione Palati, ad Capita bubulo, ubi nunc sacrarium habet, aliquanto post quam excessit constitutum.
question: Quibus consulibus natum esse Augustum Suetonius tradit?

author: Tacitus
source_text: Hanc oram novissimi maris tunc primum Romana classis circumvecta insulam esse Britanniam adfirmavit, ac simul incognitas ad id tempus insulas, quas Orcadas vocant, invenit domuitque.
question: Quid Romana classis, oram novissimi maris circumvecta, tum primum adfirmavit?
question_en: What did the Roman fleet, having sailed around the coast of the farthest sea, then for the first time affirm?
derivation: The classic discovery under Agricola's governorship: the circumnavigating fleet confirmed Britain is an island ('insulam esse Britanniam adfirmavit'). Indirect statement (acc.+inf.) answer supported verbatim; entity-anchored to Britannia + the Roman fleet; one of the most-cited facts of the Agricola.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Hanc oram novissimi maris tunc primum Romana classis circumvecta insulam esse Britanniam adfirmavit, ac simul incognitas ad id tempus insulas, quas Orcadas vocant, invenit domuitque.
question: Quas insulas, antea incognitas, Romana classis Britanniam circumvecta invenit domuitque?
question_en: Which previously unknown islands did the Roman fleet discover and subdue while sailing around Britain?
derivation: Distinct fact from the same sentence: the fleet discovered and subdued the Orcades ('insulas, quas Orcadas vocant, invenit domuitque'). Anchored to the Roman fleet's circumnavigation; single named-islands answer verbatim.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Igitur primus omnium Romanorum divus Iulius cum exercitu Britanniam ingressus, quamquam prospera pugna terruerit incolas ac litore potitus sit, potest videri ostendisse posteris, non tradidisse.
question: Quis primus omnium Romanorum cum exercitu Britanniam ingressus est?
question_en: Who was the first of all Romans to enter Britain with an army?
derivation: States verbatim that Julius Caesar was 'primus omnium Romanorum' to enter Britain with an army. Single named answer; closed-book, much-cited historical fact; anchored to Britannia + the Romans.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Consularium primus Aulus Plautius praepositus ac subinde Ostorius Scapula, uterque bello egregius: redactaque paulatim in formam provinciae proxima pars Britanniae, addita insuper veteranorum colonia.
question: Quis primus ex consularibus Britanniae praepositus est?
question_en: Who was the first of the consulars placed in charge of Britain?
derivation: Named office/relation: 'Consularium primus Aulus Plautius praepositus'. Anchored to Britannia; single named answer verbatim; closed-book.

author: Tacitus
source_text: His atque talibus in vicem instincti, Boudicca generis regii femina duce (neque enim sexum in imperiis discernunt) sumpsere universi bellum.
question: Qua femina duce Britanni adversus Romanos universi bellum sumpserunt?
question_en: Under which woman as leader did the Britons all together take up war against the Romans?
derivation: Names the leader of the British revolt, 'Boudicca generis regii femina duce'. Anchored to the Britons + Romans; single named answer verbatim (spelled 'Boudicca' in the text); famous, closed-book.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Igitur praemissa classe, quae pluribus locis praedata magnum et incertum terrorem faceret, expedito exercitu, cui ex Britannis fortissimos et longa pace exploratos addiderat, ad montem Graupium pervenit, quem iam hostis insederat.
question: Ad quem montem Agricola pervenit, ubi postremum cum Britannis proelium commisit?
question_en: To what mountain did Agricola come, where he fought his final battle with the Britons?
derivation: The climactic battle's site, 'ad montem Graupium pervenit'. Anchored to Agricola + the Britons; single named-place answer verbatim; the canonical battle of the Agricola.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Iamque super triginta milia armatorum aspiciebantur, et adhuc adfluebat omnis iuventus et quibus cruda ac viridis senectus, clari bello et sua quisque decora gestantes, cum inter pluris duces virtute et genere praestans nomine Calgacus apud contractam multitudinem proelium poscentem in hunc modum locutus fertur.
question: Quis dux Britannorum, virtute et genere praestans, ante proelium ad montem Graupium orationem habuisse fertur?
question_en: Which leader of the Britons, outstanding in valor and birth, is said to have delivered a speech before the battle at Mons Graupius?
derivation: Names the Caledonian leader, 'nomine Calgacus'. Anchored to the Britons + Mons Graupius; single named answer verbatim. The question concerns only the speaker's identity (a fact), not the rhetorical content of the speech. 'fertur... locutus' mirrors the source's report-frame; closed-book and famous.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Caesa hostium ad decem milia: nostrorum trecenti sexaginta cecidere, in quis Aulus Atticus praefectus cohortis, iuvenili ardore et ferocia equi hostibus inlatus.
question: Quot Romani in proelio ad montem Graupium ceciderunt, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: How many Romans fell in the battle at Mons Graupius, as Tacitus records?
derivation: Number fact: Roman dead at Mons Graupius, 'nostrorum trecenti sexaginta cecidere' (against about 10,000 of the enemy). Anchored to the named battle; single number answer verbatim; 'ut Tacitus tradit' marks the closed-book authorial frame.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Germania omnis a Gallis Raetisque et Pannoniis Rheno et Danuvio fluminibus, a Sarmatis Dacisque mutuo metu aut montibus separatur
question: Quibus fluminibus Germaniam a Gallis Raetisque et Pannoniis separari Tacitus tradit?
question_en: By which rivers does Tacitus report that Germania is separated from the Gauls, Raeti, and Pannonii?
answer_en: By the Rhine and the Danube.
derivation: Opening geographical fact. Anchored to Germania + named neighbouring peoples; two named rivers as a single verifiable answer, supported verbatim by 'Rheno et Danuvio fluminibus ... separatur'. Indirect statement (Germaniam separari) governed by tradit. Closed-book: the Rhine/Danube bounds of Germania are a stock fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Celebrant carminibus antiquis, quod unum apud illos memoriae et annalium genus est, Tuistonem deum terra editum.
question: Quem deum terra editum Germani carminibus antiquis celebrant, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which earth-born god do the Germani celebrate in ancient songs, as Tacitus reports?
derivation: The Germanic origin-myth. Anchored to Germani + Tacitus; single named theonym, supported verbatim by 'Tuistonem deum terra editum'. Tuistonem accusative as object of celebrant. Closed-book: Tuisto is the famous earth-born god of Germania.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Ei filium Mannum, originem gentis conditoremque, Manno tris filios adsignant, e quorum nominibus proximi Oceano Ingaevones, medii Herminones, ceteri Istaevones vocentur.
question: Quem filium Tuistonis Germani originem gentis conditoremque appellant, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which son of Tuisto do the Germani call the origin and founder of their race, per Tacitus?
derivation: Second link of the origin-myth. Anchored to Tuisto's son; single named answer, supported verbatim by 'Ei filium Mannum, originem gentis conditoremque'. Mannum accusative as object of appellant. Closed-book: Mannus as founder of the Germani is a stock fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Deorum maxime Mercurium colunt, cui certis diebus humanis quoque hostiis litare fas habent.
question: Quem deorum Germanos maxime colere Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which of the gods does Tacitus report the Germani worship most?
derivation: The chief cult-fact of the Germania. Anchored to Germani + Tacitus; single named god, supported verbatim by 'Deorum maxime Mercurium colunt'. Indirect statement (Germanos colere) governed by tradit; Mercurium accusative.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Vidimus sub divo Vespasiano Veledam diu apud plerosque numinis loco habitam; sed et olim Albrunam et compluris alias venerati sunt, non adulatione nec tamquam facerent deas.
question: Quam feminam sub divo Vespasiano numinis loco habitam esse Tacitus testatur?
question_en: Which woman does Tacitus testify was held in the place of a divinity under the deified Vespasian?
derivation: Named prophetess, dated to a named emperor. Anchored to Vespasian; single named-person answer, supported verbatim by 'Vidimus sub divo Vespasiano Veledam ... numinis loco habitam'. Indirect statement (Veledam habitam esse) governed by testatur.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Rari gladiis aut maioribus lanceis utuntur: hastas vel ipsorum vocabulo frameas gerunt angusto et brevi ferro
question: Quo proprio vocabulo Germani hastas suas appellant, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: By what native term do the Germani call their spears, per Tacitus?
derivation: Named weapon-custom. Anchored to Germani + Tacitus; single Germanic term, supported verbatim by 'hastas vel ipsorum vocabulo frameas gerunt'. Frameas accusative plural as object of appellant. Closed-book: the framea is Tacitus's well-known native word.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Nec dierum numerum, ut nos, sed noctium computant.
question: Utrum dierum an noctium numerum Germanos computare Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Does Tacitus report that the Germani reckon time by the count of days or of nights?
derivation: Distinctive time-reckoning custom. Anchored to Germani + Tacitus; single verifiable answer, supported verbatim by 'sed noctium computant'. Indirect statement (Germanos computare) governed by tradit. Famous closed-book fact (origin of 'fortnight'-style night-counting).

author: Tacitus
source_text: Nullas Germanorum populis urbes habitari satis notum est, ne pati quidem inter se iunctas sedes.
question: Quot urbes a Germanorum populis habitari Tacitus tradit?
question_en: How many cities does Tacitus report were inhabited by the Germanic peoples?
derivation: The absence of cities. Anchored to Germanic peoples + Tacitus; single verifiable answer, supported verbatim by 'Nullas Germanorum populis urbes habitari satis notum est'. Closed-book: that the Germani had no cities is a stock ethnographic fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: At Germani Carbone et Cassio et Scauro Aurelio et Servilio Caepione Gnaeoque Mallio fusis vel captis quinque simul consularis exercitus populo Romano, Varum trisque cum eo legiones etiam Caesari abstulerunt
question: Quot legiones Germani una cum Varo Caesari abstulerunt, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: How many legions, together with Varus, did the Germani take from Caesar (Augustus), as Tacitus reports?
derivation: The Varus disaster, a famous number fact. Anchored to Varus + the Germani; single number answer, supported verbatim by 'Varum trisque cum eo legiones etiam Caesari abstulerunt'. Closed-book: the loss of three legions in the Teutoburg defeat is among the best-known facts of Roman history.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Sescentesimum et quadragesimum annum urbs nostra agebat, cum primum Cimbrorum audita sunt arma, Caecilio Metello et Papirio Carbone consulibus.
question: Quibus consulibus primum Cimbrorum arma audita esse Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Under which consuls does Tacitus say the arms of the Cimbri were first heard of?
answer_en: Under Caecilius Metellus and Papirius Carbo.
derivation: Dating of the first Cimbric war by named consuls. Anchored to the Cimbri; two named consuls as the verifiable answer, supported verbatim by the ablative absolute 'Caecilio Metello et Papirio Carbone consulibus'. Indirect statement (arma audita esse) governed by tradit.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Insigne gentis obliquare crinem nodoque substringere: sic Suebi a ceteris Germanis, sic Sueborum ingenui a servis separantur.
question: Quod est insigne Sueborum, quo a ceteris Germanis separantur, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: What is the distinctive mark of the Suebi, by which they are set apart from the other Germani, according to Tacitus?
answer_en: To twist the hair sideways and bind it in a knot.
derivation: The Suebian hair-knot. Anchored to the Suebi vs. other Germani; the answer mirrors the source phrase 'obliquare crinem nodoque substringere'. Closed-book: the Suebenknoten is the signature custom of the Suebi in Tacitus.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Fortissimus quisque ferreum insuper anulum (ignominiosum id genti) velut vinculum gestat, donec se caede hostis absolvat.
question: Quid ferreum apud Chattos fortissimus quisque velut vinculum gestat, donec hostem caedat, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: What iron object does each bravest Chattus wear like a fetter until he slays an enemy, per Tacitus?
derivation: Named Chattan custom. Anchored to the Chatti; concrete object answer, supported verbatim by 'ferreum ... anulum ... velut vinculum gestat, donec se caede hostis absolvat'. Closed-book: the Chatti's iron ring of dishonour, worn until a first kill, is a distinctive Tacitean detail.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Sed et mare scrutantur, ac soli omnium sucinum, quod ipsi glesum vocant, inter vada atque in ipso litore legunt.
question: Quo nomine Aestii sucinum, quod soli omnium legunt, appellant, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: By what name do the Aestii call amber (sucinum), which alone of all peoples they gather, per Tacitus?
derivation: The Aestii and amber. Anchored to the Aestii (named in the same chapter as the only amber-gatherers, 'soli omnium'); single native term as answer, supported verbatim by 'sucinum, quod ipsi glesum vocant'. Spelling 'glesum'/'sucinum' kept as in the text. Closed-book: the amber-gathering Aestii are a stock fact.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Suionibus Sitonum gentes continuantur. Cetera similes uno differunt, quod femina dominatur; in tantum non modo a libertate sed etiam a servitute degenerant.
question: Quo uno Sitones a Suionibus differre Tacitus tradit?
question_en: In what one respect does Tacitus say the Sitones differ from the Suiones?
answer_en: In that a woman rules them.
derivation: The woman-ruled tribe. Anchored to the Sitones vs. the Suiones; single verifiable point of difference, supported verbatim by 'uno differunt, quod femina dominatur'. Sitones accusative (subject of differre) governed by tradit.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Fennis mira feritas, foeda paupertas: non arma, non equi, non penates; victui herba, vestitui pelles, cubile humus: solae in sagittis spes, quas inopia ferri ossibus asperant.
question: Quibus rebus Fenni, ferri inopia, sagittas suas asperant, ut Tacitus tradit?
question_en: With what do the Fenni tip their arrows, for lack of iron, per Tacitus?
derivation: Named custom of the Fenni. Anchored to the Fenni; concrete material answer, supported verbatim by 'solae in sagittis spes, quas inopia ferri ossibus asperant'. Closed-book: bone-tipped arrows of the iron-poor Fenni are a distinctive Tacitean detail.

author: Tacitus
source_text: Reudigni deinde et Aviones et Anglii et Varini et Eudoses et Suardones et Nuithones fluminibus aut silvis muniuntur. Nec quicquam notabile in singulis, nisi quod in commune Nerthum, id est Terram matrem, colunt eamque intervenire rebus hominum, invehi populis arbitrantur.
question: Quam deam, id est Terram matrem, Reudignos ceterasque gentes in commune colere Tacitus tradit?
question_en: Which goddess, that is Mother Earth, does Tacitus report the Reudigni and the other tribes worship in common?
derivation: Named deity of the Ingaevonic tribes. Anchored to the named group (Reudigni, Aviones, Anglii, etc.); single theonym answer, supported verbatim by 'Nerthum, id est Terram matrem, colunt'. Nerthum accusative; indirect statement governed by tradit. Closed-book: the Nerthus cult is a famous Tacitean datum.
